title: Trump's Rights Messaging Continued to Be Pressured by Amnesty's Pattern Evidence
description_short: Trump's Rights Messaging Continued to Be Pressured by Amnesty's Pattern Evidence
description_medium: Amnesty International published an assessment of human-rights concerns during Donald Trump’s first 100 days in office. The available packet does not identify the policies or affected groups the report analyzed, the standards it applied, or the findings supporting a pattern across cases. It also gives no Trump statement showing that the report changed his public messaging.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Rights Messaging Continued to Be Pressured by Amnesty's Pattern Evidence
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Rights Messaging Continued to Be Pressured by Amnesty's Pattern Evidence

notes: Needs context: the Amnesty page returned HTTP 403, and the packet supplies only the report’s broad first-100-days framing. It lacks the organizations, policies, affected groups, standards and findings, as well as a matching Trump statement. Proposed correction: identify specific report findings and any response, or describe the assessment without claiming it changed messaging.

title: Trump's Full-Disclosure Claims Continued to Clash With AP's Quantified Gaps
description_short: Trump's Full-Disclosure Claims Continued to Clash With AP's Quantified Gaps
description_medium: The Associated Press reported that at least 16 files were no longer visible on a Justice Department webpage for Jeffrey Epstein-related documents. That count concerns public access to the page; it does not establish that the underlying records were destroyed or identify who changed the webpage. The packet does not quote a Trump promise covering those specific files.
description_long: On December 20, 2025, the Associated Press reported that at least 16 files had disappeared from a Justice Department webpage containing Jeffrey Epstein-related documents. The number describes files no longer visible to the public on that page; it does not establish that the underlying records were deleted from government custody. The supplied materials do not identify the files individually, date each disappearance, name the person who changed the page or include the department’s explanation. They also do not quote a specific Trump statement promising the release of those same documents. A countable change in webpage content and a promise about disclosure are separate facts until the documents and the wording of the promise are matched. The report therefore supports describing a reported gap in public access, while leaving its cause and responsibility unresolved. It does not by itself prove that Trump’s full-disclosure claims were false or that he directed the page changes.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Full-Disclosure Claims Continued to Clash With AP's Quantified Gaps
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Full-Disclosure Claims Continued to Clash With AP's Quantified Gaps

notes: Needs context: the AP report page returned HTTP 403; its headline says at least 16 files disappeared from a DOJ webpage. The packet lacks file identities, removal dates, the DOJ explanation, and a Trump disclosure statement covering these files. Proposed correction: report the webpage gap without claiming it proves a contradiction or presidential direction.

title: Immigration Social Media Vetting - Comprehensive Digital Surveillance System
description_short: Immigration Social Media Vetting - Comprehensive Digital Surveillance System
description_medium: In April 2025, USCIS announced social-media screening of immigrants for content the administration considered antisemitic. A State Department cable separately instructed consulates to vet visa applicants with a presence in Gaza since January 1, 2007. TechPolicy.Press also described ICE web-scraping and a Palantir contract. These were distinct policies and tools, not evidence of one system monitoring every immigrant.
description_long: In March and April 2025, the administration expanded several different forms of immigration-related screening and data collection. TechPolicy.Press described Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s “Catch and Revoke” effort targeting foreign nationals said to support Hamas or other designated groups, and reported that ICE used ShadowDragon to gather data from more than 200 websites and social platforms. On April 9, USCIS announced social-media screening of immigrants for content it considered antisemitic. A State Department cable reported a week later separately instructed consulates to vet visa applicants who had been present in Gaza since January 1, 2007. The article also discussed Palantir contracting and concerns about privacy and political expression. These actions involved different agencies, populations and purposes. The available reporting does not show continuous surveillance of all immigrants, an AI system reviewing every account, or one comprehensive program linking the tools. The policies raise questions about screening and expression, but the available accounts do not establish one all-encompassing program.

preserved_fields.title: Immigration Social Media Vetting - Comprehensive Digital Surveillance System
preserved_fields.description_short: Immigration Social Media Vetting - Comprehensive Digital Surveillance System

notes: Needs context: the accessible TechPolicy.Press account describes separate screening and data-collection efforts, while AP returned HTTP 403. The sources do not establish continuous monitoring of every immigrant or a single comprehensive system. Proposed correction: describe the separate policies, populations and agencies. The original category was not canonical, so it is set to Authoritarianism.

title: Trump's Unthinkable Trajectory Frame Kept Oversight Windows Compressed Under High-Impact Decisions
description_short: Trump's Unthinkable Trajectory Frame Kept Oversight Windows Compressed Under High-Impact Decisions
description_medium: The Atlantic’s “Unthinkable” project looks back at 50 episodes from Trump’s first term that it selected as norm-bending or destructive. Its examples include Trump praising a congressman who assaulted a reporter and an inaccurate White House crowd-size claim. The retrospective does not identify a March 2026 decision or document a shortened oversight timeline.
description_long: The Atlantic’s “Unthinkable” project gathers 50 episodes from Donald Trump’s first term that its editors considered improbable, norm-bending or destructive. Examples include Trump praising a congressman who had body-slammed a reporter and a White House press secretary’s inaccurate claim about the inauguration crowd. The project offers a retrospective account of earlier controversies and the magazine’s interpretation of them. It does not describe a March 2026 high-impact decision, identify an oversight body, or give a timeline showing that review was compressed. Nor does the collection show that its framing affected the administration’s decision process. Earlier episodes may be relevant to a discussion of executive norms, but they cannot establish how much time officials had to scrutinize a later action. That would require a specific decision, records of the review process and evidence about when oversight occurred. The linked project supports an account of the retrospective, not a finding about a current oversight window.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Unthinkable Trajectory Frame Kept Oversight Windows Compressed Under High-Impact Decisions
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Unthinkable Trajectory Frame Kept Oversight Windows Compressed Under High-Impact Decisions

notes: Needs context: the Atlantic link is a retrospective of first-term episodes, returned HTTP 403 and does not identify a March 2026 decision or review timeline. Proposed correction: recast this as a retrospective or cite the specific decision and oversight records behind the claim.

title: Trump's Promise Absolutism Narrative Sustained Long-Tail Credibility Risk Across Repeated Review Cycles
description_short: Trump's Promise Absolutism Narrative Sustained Long-Tail Credibility Risk Across Repeated Review Cycles
description_medium: Before Trump’s March 4, 2026, State of the Union, PBS reported that he said he had kept all his campaign promises. PolitiFact’s tracker covered 75 second-term pledges: about 19% were marked kept, 45% in progress and 31% stalled. The snapshot tests the breadth of his claim, but does not measure lasting effects on public trust.
description_long: PBS NewsHour reported on March 4, 2026, that Donald Trump said he had kept all his campaign promises. PolitiFact’s second-term Promise Meter tracked 75 pledges; at that time, about 19% were marked “Promise Kept,” 45% “In the Works” and 31% “Stalled,” with the remainder listed as compromises or broken. These labels describe the tracker’s status on that date, not a final audit: policies can change, and PolitiFact evaluates measurable outcomes rather than stated intentions. Examples included a limited tax break for older people rather than Trump’s broader promise about Social Security taxes, and his pledge to end the Russia–Ukraine war within 24 hours, which had not been met by its stated deadline. The figures show a difference between an unqualified claim of completion and the tracker’s snapshot, where most items were not marked kept. They do not establish how the statement affected public confidence over later review cycles. The reporting does not track public response over time, so it cannot show whether credibility changed across later review cycles.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Promise Absolutism Narrative Sustained Long-Tail Credibility Risk Across Repeated Review Cycles
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Promise Absolutism Narrative Sustained Long-Tail Credibility Risk Across Repeated Review Cycles

notes: Needs context: the PBS/PolitiFact snapshot supports comparison with Trump’s statement, but does not establish a lasting credibility effect across later review cycles. Proposed correction: retain the dated promise-status comparison and omit the long-term consequence unless audience evidence is available.
